schedule:
In this semester, students will write three separate drafts which we will peer review as a group a week after the draft has been turned in. The first draft, in April, should be 5 pages; the second draft, in May, will be 10 pages; the third draft, in June, will be 15 pages.

Students should work towards a viable thesis statement that they can support in a twenty-page paper. Students should work on making sure that each paragraph in their paper begins with a claim that they then support with analyzed evidence.
scorePolicy:
In the spring semester students' grades depend mainly on their participation, with some attention, also, to the quality of their work. To receive a higher grade, students should do the following:
1) Turn in their drafts on time (by the agreed-upon deadline)
2) Do a strong peer review of each other's work and give helpful feedback during our meeting
3) Make progress between each draft, showing that they have paid attention to the comments received. The professor and the students' peers should not need to make the same comments twice--because the student will have made the necessary revisions between drafts.

Naturally, students must also pay attention to correct citation and avoid plagiarism and patchwriting.

The purpose of this course is to guide our students to explore their interested field, to look for possible critical approaches, to locate intriguing issues, to map out the various aspects pertaining to the discussions on certain topic, and to work out an outline that will eventually lead to the completion of an MLA-styled academic paper.
